summary: Updates SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to clarify which form of internationalized domain names is used, U-labels or A-labels, in email authentication. These specifications publish information in DNS. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Domain names can be written in other alphabets, and email checks must agree which form to use.

questions: should dkim use u-labels or a-labels
does spf work with internationalized domain names
subtitle: Settles which form of an internationalized domain name SPF, DKIM and DMARC must use, so mail with non-ASCII addresses can be authenticated.

tldr.problem: SPF, DKIM and DMARC were written when every domain name in mail was ASCII. Internationalized mail can carry domain names as U-labels or A-labels, and the specifications did not say clearly which to use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says that names are converted to A-labels before DNS lookups, that data stored in DNS stays ASCII, and that DKIM signatures in internationalized messages should use U-labels. It also relaxes the DKIM quoting rules for UTF-8.
tldr.outcome: Senders and receivers can write interoperable code for authenticating internationalized mail. The RFC updates RFC 6376, RFC 7208 and RFC 7489.

today: RFC 8616 is a Proposed Standard and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6376, RFC 7208 and RFC 7489.

sections.title: Why Authentication Needs Updating
sections.content:
Three email authentication systems let a domain owner publish information in the DNS. SPF (RFC 7208) publishes which host addresses may send mail for a domain. DKIM (RFC 6376) puts cryptographic signatures on messages, with the validation keys published in the DNS. DMARC (RFC 7489) publishes policy about the domain in the From: header field.

In conventional email, every domain name is ASCII, and internationalized domain names appear as A-labels in header fields, SMTP sessions and the DNS. Internationalized mail, generally called EAI (Email Address Internationalization), allows U-labels in SMTP sessions and in message header fields, and UTF-8 in the local part of mailbox names.

Every U-label is equivalent to an A-label, so in principle there is no ambiguity. In practice, using one consistent form makes it more likely that sender and receiver code interoperates. That is the gap this RFC fills.
sections.eli5: The same name can be written in two ways, a fancy way and a plain way. Everyone needs to pick the same way when they check it, or the check might not match.

sections.title: Definitions and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC uses IDN (Internationalized Domain Name) to mean a domain name containing either U-labels or A-labels. It uses the requirement words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in BCP 14.

One caveat is stated up front: DMARC is not a Standards Track protocol, so for DMARC this specification gives advice rather than requirements. For SPF and DKIM it states requirements.
sections.eli5: For two of the three checks the rules are firm. For the third, the document only gives friendly advice, because that third one is not an official standard yet.

sections.title: General Principles
sections.content:
In the headers of EAI messages, domain names that used to be ASCII-only can be U-labels, and mailbox local parts can be UTF-8. Header field names and other text meant mainly for computers rather than people stay ASCII.

Strings stored in DNS records also stay ASCII, because there is no way to tell whether a client retrieving a record expects an EAI or an ASCII result. When a domain name from a header field includes U-labels, those labels are translated to A-labels before the DNS lookup, as RFC 5891 describes.

The rule of thumb: people-facing text may be internationalized, but anything stored in the DNS or looked up in the DNS is ASCII.
sections.eli5: People can see the fancy spelling, but the phone book only has the plain spelling. So you translate to plain before you look anything up.

sections.title: SPF and Internationalized Mail
sections.content:
SPF uses two identities from the SMTP session: the host name in the EHLO command and the domain in the address of the MAIL FROM command. Because EHLO comes before the server says whether it supports the SMTPUTF8 extension, an IDN host name in EHLO MUST be represented as A-labels. An IDN in MAIL FROM can be either U-labels or A-labels.

All U-labels MUST be converted to A-labels before SPF validation. This covers the name used for the original DNS lookup and the names produced by macro expansion of domain-spec. Names inside an SPF DNS record must still be A-labels, a rule that is unchanged because any SPF record may authorize either EAI or conventional mail.

The macros %{s} and %{l} expand the local part of the sender's mailbox. If the local part contains non-ASCII characters, terms that use them match nothing, because such local parts cannot be DNS labels. The RFC notes these macros are rarely used, so this is unlikely to be a problem in practice.
sections.eli5: When the mail server checks who is allowed to send, it first turns any fancy-spelled name into the plain spelling. If a name part cannot be turned into plain letters, that one special rule simply never matches.

sections.title: DKIM and Internationalized Mail
sections.content:
DKIM has a header field holding a signature and a DNS record holding the validation key. For internationalized header fields, the RFC makes three changes.

  • The dkim-safe-char rule of dkim-quoted-printable is replaced so that non-ASCII UTF-8 characters (UTF8-2, UTF8-3, UTF8-4 from RFC 3629) no longer need quoting.
  • Domain names in the d=, i= and s= tags of a DKIM-Signature header field, which RFC 6376 required to be A-labels, SHOULD now be U-labels in internationalized message header fields. A-labels remain valid to allow a transition from older software. The local part of an i= tag may use the extended characters of RFC 6532.
  • When computing or verifying the hash, the signer or verifier MUST use the domain name in the format in which it occurs in the header field.

Relaxed header canonicalization lowercases header field names. Since field names are printable ASCII, that remains plain ASCII case conversion. DKIM key records contain no domain names, so they do not change.
sections.eli5: A signature is like a wax seal made from the exact words on the letter. So the seal is made from the name exactly as written on the letter, fancy letters and all, and the signer may now write names with fancy letters.

sections.title: DMARC and Internationalized Mail
sections.content:
DMARC defines a policy language that domain owners set for the domain of the address in the RFC5322.From header field. RFC 7489 described somewhat imprecisely how IDNs in that domain are handled. This RFC updates Section 6.6.1 and Section 7.1 of RFC 7489 to say that all U-labels in the domains being handled are converted to A-labels before further processing.

DMARC policy records can contain email addresses in the rua and ruf tags. A policy record can serve both internationalized and conventional mail, so those addresses still have to be conventional addresses, not internationalized ones.

As noted in the scope section, because DMARC is not a Standards Track protocol, this part is advice rather than a requirement.
sections.eli5: For the policy notes, names are again turned into the plain spelling first. And the addresses where reports are sent must be plain ones, so every mail system can read them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that email faces a vast range of threats and abuses. It attempts to mitigate some of them slightly and, as far as the author knows, adds no new ones. The goal is for SPF, DKIM and DMARC to work as reliably on internationalized mail as on ASCII mail, so that applications built on them, such as some mail filters that catch spam and phish, work more reliably.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The point is to make the safety checks work just as well for mail in other alphabets as for plain English mail. Nothing new is opened up for bad guys.
